I'm on chapter three, and this book is phenomenal. I don't know where I heard about it - it was either suggested to me here, or I saw the title on RvF.

If you've ever delved into the Germanic occult, or read up on modern heathenry, Wiccanism, and the like, you no doubt have come across the concept of "spells". Well, there's a lot of pop culture bullshit mixed in with all that stuff these days, but at its core, the idea is the alteration of oneself through the use of meditation aided by smells, textures, sights and sounds to solidify the experience.

Eastern traditions teach meditation as a matter of course in a more ascetic sense. In particular, the one of my favorite passages in the Hagakure addresses this specifically:

Meditation on inevitable death should be performed daily. Every day when one's body and mind are at peace, one should meditate upon being ripped apart by arrows, rifles, spears and swords, being carried away by surging waves, being thrown into the midst of a great fire, being struck by lightning, being shaken to death by a great earthquake, falling from thousand-foot cliffs, dying of disease or committing seppuku at the death of one's master. And every day without fail one should consider himself as dead.

I actually did this before I went into the army. It alleviated a tremendous amount of anxiety, allowing me to sleep for the first time in 4 days.

The redskins used a sort of guided vision quest to achieve wisdom and insight. The quests consisted of heavy use of incenses (smells), firelight and shadow (sights), clothing (textures) and rhythms (sounds).

All of these traditions, which wouldn't have persisted if they didn't work to a measurable extent, have revolved around some form of visualization of the goal - with special attention being paid to the little details, like smells, sights and sounds, to form a practice experience, instead of just a picture in your head. And that's what this book talks about. But it offers clinical insight into how this visualization aids in the achievement of our goals, and how everything about oneself is tied to our self-image. And that self-image can be changed.
